english-prompts__1.answer: 90-second pitch. Structure. 'I'm a senior frontend engineer with [N] years of experience, currently at [company] where I focus on [domain — fintech / e-commerce / SaaS]. My main areas of strength are [pick 2-3: real-time UI, performance engineering, frontend architecture, design systems]. In my recent work I [highlight one or two concrete achievements with numbers — led migration to microfrontends, optimized critical-path performance with measurable improvement, built design system used across teams]. What I'm looking for next is [serious technical scope, real-time challenges, fintech domain] — which is why I'm excited about this role.' Avoid: chronological CV-walkthrough, mentioning university, generic statements. Make it feel natural, not memorized. Practice out loud — fluency matters more than vocabulary.

english-prompts__2.answer: Show you've done research. Structure. (1) Specific things that caught your attention: 'Exness is a serious trading platform with millions of active users — that means real-time UI with strict performance requirements, which is exactly the area I want to grow in.' (2) Tech alignment: 'I've seen mentions of microfrontends and React in your stack — that aligns with how I want to evolve as an engineer.' (3) Domain interest: 'Fintech sits at this interesting intersection of technical depth and real business impact — when frontend lags, traders lose money on slippage. That kind of impact is meaningful to me.' (4) Optional personal: 'A friend who works there mentioned the engineering culture is solid.' Avoid: 'great company, international, good benefits' — generic. Be specific.

english-prompts__3.answer: Treat as a product pitch. Structure. (1) Context: 'I work on [product type] at [company-scale]. The product serves [users] and the frontend handles [scale — millions of MAU, real-time data, complex state].' (2) Your role: 'I own [area] — for example the [feature]. End-to-end: design, implementation, performance, monitoring.' (3) Concrete recent work: 'Recently I [specific thing — led a migration, built X, optimized Y] with [outcome — numbers if possible].' (4) Technical decisions: 'One decision I'm proud of is [trade-off you made and why].' Practice the technical vocabulary out loud: render bypass, state machine, optimistic update, sequence numbers, exponential backoff. Senior recruiters expect fluent technical English.

english-prompts__4.answer: STAR format works in English too. 'The biggest technical challenge I've faced was [project]. The context was [scale and constraints — for example, real-time trading UI with thousands of updates per second]. The challenge was that [specific hard problem — naive setState approach caused render storm; main thread was blocked]. My approach was [decisions — buffer updates with requestAnimationFrame, render-bypass through refs for high-frequency cells, virtualize the list]. The result was [measurable — p95 INP dropped from 350ms to 120ms; UI stayed responsive under 1k ticks per second]. Looking back, the key lesson was [insight — measure before optimizing; render-bypass is a valid escape hatch when React rerenders are too expensive].' Numbers and specifics make this credible; avoid vague 'it was complex' phrasing.

english-prompts__5.answer: Show architectural thinking. Structure. (1) Set the stage: 'On my recent project we had [scale — multiple product teams, microfrontend setup, complex state across domains].' (2) The architecture: 'We had a host application that owned navigation, auth, and routing, with several remotes for product domains [orders, users, reports]. They were composed at runtime using Module Federation. Shared dependencies — React, design system, auth context — were singletons.' (3) Trade-offs: 'The main trade-off was version skew between remotes — we mitigated with strict version requirements and integration smoke tests in CI. Independent deploys saved coordination overhead but added observability complexity.' (4) Outcome: 'Deploy frequency went up 3x, blast radius of incidents went down significantly.' Use proper terms: host, remote, Module Federation, version skew, blast radius.

english-prompts__6.answer: Show methodical thinking. 'My approach is to start from the symptom and narrow down. First, I confirm the bug reliably reproduces — without that, debugging is guesswork. Then I form hypotheses about what could cause it, ranked by likelihood. I test each hypothesis with the cheapest verification first — checking recent commits, looking at the network tab, console errors, profiler. I bisect when possible — git bisect, or toggling features off. I keep a running note of what I've ruled out, so I don't go in circles. For tricky bugs in production I rely on observability — Sentry stack traces with source maps, RUM data, breadcrumbs from user sessions. The most important habit I've built is to confirm the fix actually addresses the root cause, not just makes the symptom go away — that's how regressions sneak back in.'

english-prompts__7.answer: Choose a real story but frame constructively. 'There was a time when a teammate and I disagreed about [technical decision — for example, whether to use Redux or React Query for new server state]. The disagreement was getting circular in PR comments, so I suggested we have a sync conversation. I started by listening — what concerns was he trying to address? I shared my reasoning with concrete examples. We realized we were optimizing for different things — he was prioritizing consistency with the legacy code, I was prioritizing simpler API for the new flow. We landed on a hybrid: React Query for server state in new modules, Redux preserved for the legacy global UI state, with a documented migration plan. Lesson: most disagreements are about priorities, not facts. The fastest path to resolution is making those priorities explicit.' Show emotional maturity, not winning.

english-prompts__8.answer: Show you push back constructively. 'On a recent project, the product team wanted to ship a new feature without proper analytics tracking. I disagreed — without analytics, we couldn't tell if the feature was working. I didn't just object — I drafted a short note showing two examples of past features where lack of tracking had cost us time, and proposed adding three concrete events that would cover the main user paths. I shared it with the PM async, then we discussed it briefly. The PM agreed it was a small cost relative to the visibility we'd get. The feature shipped with tracking, and within a week the data showed our hypothesis was wrong about user behavior — we adjusted before fully rolling out. The lesson: pushback works best when you bring an alternative, not just an objection.' Show data-driven, collaborative, not adversarial.

english-prompts__9.answer: Show comfort with ambiguity — a senior signal. 'My approach is to make the unclear parts explicit early. I start by writing down what I think the requirements are, in my own words, and check that with the PM or design — that surfaces about 80% of misunderstandings in the first conversation. For the parts that are still unclear, I separate what I can decide myself from what needs alignment. I bias toward making reversible decisions quickly — if something is a two-way door, I just pick a reasonable option and move. For one-way doors I invest more upfront. I write short ADRs even for moderate decisions, so the team can see my reasoning. And I share early prototypes — getting feedback on a 30%-complete version is faster than refining requirements abstractly.' Show structure, not paralysis.

english-prompts__10.answer: Show ability to translate. 'My approach is to translate technical concepts into business outcomes. Instead of saying we have technical debt in the order flow, I say something like — every new feature in this area takes about 2x longer to ship because of accumulated complexity, and we've shipped three regressions in the last quarter that cost us X support hours. That gives PMs a number they can compare against feature work. I also use analogies when helpful — calling rebuilding the foundation while the house is on fire is more memorable than refactoring the state management. The other thing I try to do is offer options with explicit trade-offs, not single recommendations. Saying we can do A — fast but risky, or B — slower but stable, lets the PM make an informed call rather than just trusting me.' Show empathy and clarity.

english-prompts__11.answer: 'For me, ownership means thinking about the full lifecycle of what I build, not just the part I'm assigned. If I'm working on a feature, that means I think about how it'll be deployed, monitored, debugged at 3am if it breaks, maintained two years from now when I'm not the only one touching it. It also means I don't wait for someone to tell me about a problem — if I notice something that's wrong, even outside my immediate work, I either fix it or surface it. The third part is I take responsibility for outcomes, not just outputs — shipping something that doesn't actually solve the problem isn't success. Concretely, that shows up in how I work: writing observability into features from day one, leaving documentation for future maintainers, following up after a launch to see if metrics actually moved.' Concrete behavior, not abstract.

english-prompts__12.answer: 'I think mentoring is mostly about creating the space for someone to learn, not telling them what to do. When I work with junior or mid-level engineers, I try to ask questions before giving answers — what have you tried, what do you think the problem is. Often they figure it out themselves with a small nudge, and they retain it better than if I just told them. For more structured mentoring, I do regular pair-programming sessions on real work — that's where most of the learning happens, in the moment of actually solving something. I also share my reasoning out loud when reviewing their code — explaining why I prefer a pattern, not just that I do. And I try to give them stretch assignments — slightly above their current level — and stay close enough to support but not rescue. Mentoring is also bidirectional — I learn from less experienced engineers all the time, especially about tools and approaches I haven't kept up with.'

english-prompts__13.answer: 'I do my best work in environments with a few specific qualities. First, psychological safety — being able to admit when I don't know something, push back on a decision, or own up to a mistake without that being held against me. Second, high standards — code review is real, not rubber-stamp; tests are expected for critical paths; performance has a budget. Third, autonomy — once trust is established, I'm given the space to make decisions in my area without needing approval for every detail. Fourth, async-first communication — I get focused work done when I have uninterrupted time blocks, and meetings are reserved for things that genuinely need synchronous discussion. And finally, sustainable pace — I do my best work over years, not in heroic sprints, and a culture that respects that pays off in retention and depth.' Show you've thought about this.

english-prompts__14.answer: Be prepared with research-backed numbers. 'Based on the market data I've reviewed for senior frontend roles in this region — looking at sources like levels.fyi, Glassdoor, and conversations with peers — I'm targeting a range of [X-Y] for the base, and I'd love to understand the full compensation package including bonus, equity if any, and benefits. That said, compensation isn't my primary driver — the technical scope and team are what made me apply here. If we're aligned on those, I'm confident we can find a number that works for both sides. Could you share the range you have for this role? That'd help me calibrate.' Avoid: throwing out a low number, refusing to share any number, sounding mercenary. Frame it as a collaborative conversation, not a negotiation battle.

english-prompts__15.answer: Stay positive. Never criticize the current employer. 'I've been at [current company] for [N years] and learned a lot — [one specific thing you genuinely value]. What I'm starting to look for now is [the thing the new role offers — bigger technical challenges, more impact, fintech domain, real-time UI, scale]. I've reached a point where the kinds of problems I want to work on aren't really available in my current role. So this isn't about leaving — it's about going somewhere I can grow into the next phase.' Avoid: complaining about manager, salary, projects. Even if true, it makes the recruiter wonder if you'd say the same about them in a year. Frame the move as forward-looking. Keep it short — 2-3 sentences max.

english-prompts__16.answer: Pick 2-3 concrete strengths with examples. 'I'd say my main strengths are: First, performance engineering — I'm comfortable using the Profiler and RUM data to find real bottlenecks and apply the right fix, whether that's memoization, virtualization, or going below React with refs and direct DOM updates for high-frequency cases. Second, complex async state — race conditions, real-time data, optimistic updates with proper rollback, sequence numbers for ordering. Third, accessibility — I treat it as part of base quality, not a checkbox; I test with keyboard and screen readers, not just axe. The thread connecting these is depth — I've gone past the surface in a few areas, and I bring that to the team through code review, ADRs, and mentoring.' Avoid generic 'I work hard' or 'I'm a team player' — say what you can actually do.

english-prompts__17.answer: Be honest, show self-awareness, frame growth. 'One area where I'm less experienced than I'd like is [specific thing — for example, deep CSS animation or backend systems]. I know this because [evidence — I've noticed I'm slower in this area, or I rely on others when this comes up]. The way I compensate is [pair-programming with specialists, reading deeply, doing side projects]. For production-critical decisions in this area, I defer to people with more depth. The other thing I'd call out — I've historically been more comfortable with focused individual work than driving large cross-team initiatives. I've been deliberately taking on more of those over the past year, and I see them as an area I'm actively growing in.' Avoid: fake-weaknesses ('I'm too perfectionist'), or weaknesses in core skills (React, TypeScript). Pick something real but adjacent.

english-prompts__18.answer: Show product-thinking, not just technical complaints. 'A few things I'd improve in my current product. First, we don't have great frontend observability — Sentry is set up but the dashboards are sparse, and we're not tracking custom domain metrics. I've been pushing for more, but it's not a priority. Second, our testing pyramid is inverted — heavy on slow, flaky e2e tests, light on integration. I'd rebalance toward integration with MSW, which gives the same confidence at much lower cost. Third, our design system is fragmented — there's a token layer, but components aren't consistent across teams. Consolidating that would save a lot of duplicated effort. The framing I bring to all of this — they're not absolute fixes, they're trade-offs the team hasn't had time to make yet, and I try to push them through influence rather than complaining.' Show you think like a product owner.

english-prompts__19.answer: This question tests opinion and reasoning. Don't be dismissive — frame trade-offs. 'A few things I think the industry over-hypes. First, microfrontends — they're real and useful, but for most teams they add infrastructure complexity that outweighs the benefit. The right time to introduce them is when you have multiple teams blocking each other on deploys, not before. Second, server components in their current form — interesting model, but the tooling and mental model still feel rough; for most apps a well-tuned SPA is fine. Third, jumping to new state management libraries every couple of years — most apps don't need anything beyond React Query plus a small store. The pattern I see is teams adopting trends because they're trending, not because they solve a problem the team actually has. The honest version of senior engineering is being willing to say no to shiny things.' Show opinions backed by reasoning.

english-prompts__20.answer: Always have 3-5 prepared questions. Match them to the interviewer. For recruiters: 'Could you walk me through what the interview process looks like from here? What's the typical timeline? What's the team I'd be joining like — size, seniority mix? What does success look like in the first six months in this role?' For tech leads / engineers: 'What are the biggest frontend challenges the team is working on right now? How are architectural decisions made — RFCs, ADRs, ad-hoc? What does code review look like in practice? What does the on-call rotation look like? What's the most painful piece of legacy you'd want a senior to help with?' Don't ask things easily answered by the company website (when was Exness founded, what countries you operate in) — that signals lack of preparation.
